title: What the venue owner adds to our keyword research

content.job: Standalone list email telling the full exchange and the collaboration principle. No offer, result claim or reply request; proposed send metadata requires WIA confirmation.
content.body:
Our team had brought the existing keywords and some proposed additions to the conversation. She explained that the shortened name was familiar to local people, as well as some couples coming from outside the area. If couples use a name like that when they talk about the area, some may use it when they search, and a keyword list put together from outside the market can miss a term like that.

The team agreed to look into her suggestion and share any additional terms they found.

It was a small exchange, but it illustrates something we value in an advertising partnership. Our team contributed the recommendations and the commitment to research. The client contributed context about how people talk about her market.

**Your firsthand knowledge of couples deserves a place alongside our advertising expertise.**

When you're already investing in Google Ads, you want the people supporting you to bring considered recommendations. You also have knowledge built through the conversations you're having with people who might choose your venue.

Those contributions can work together. The person speaking with couples can offer context that's useful to the team researching how to reach them.

We believe a recommendation should give us something meaningful to discuss with you. There should be room for your experience to contribute while we're considering the strategy, with our team taking responsibility for investigating the questions that arise.
content.ending:
If you're already investing in Google Ads, that's the kind of partnership you should expect from the team supporting you: recommendations you can trust, and a real place for what you hear from your couples.

Talk soon,
Whitney

content.title: What you hear from couples belongs in your Google Ads strategy.

slides.job: State the promise as an insight about the reader.
slides.text:
What you hear from couples belongs in your Google Ads strategy.

You hire specialists for their advertising expertise.
But the way couples describe your area is something you know firsthand, and **it deserves a seat in the keyword conversation.**

slides.job: Establish the team's contribution and invitation.
slides.text:
In a review with a venue client, we brought her current Google keywords and some recommended additions.

Then we asked whether she had questions or concerns about the terms, while the recommendations were still being considered.

slides.job: Credit the client's contribution without identifying the market.
slides.text:
She raised the shortened name people use for the region.

She explained that it was familiar to local people and to some couples coming from outside the area. Couples who say that name out loud may type it into Google, too.

slides.job: Show the team's response, stopping at the evidenced commitment.
slides.text:
We said we'd research it and send her any other terms we turned up.

She supplied the local context.
We took responsibility for investigating it, alongside the recommendations already on the table.

slides.job: Connect the exchange to an owner who already advertises.
slides.text:
If you're already advertising your venue, you have something to bring to this.

You talk with people deciding whether to get married in your area.
You hear how they describe the location and how familiar it is to them.

slides.job: Explain how the two contributions complement each other.
slides.text:
Our expertise gives the conversation a researched starting point.

Your experience adds context worth investigating.
The two play different roles, and both belong in the same discussion.

slides.job: State WIA's belief without turning one exchange into a claim about every call.
slides.text:
**We believe your firsthand knowledge deserves a real place in your advertising partnership.**

The language your couples use can help inform what we explore, while our team brings the advertising expertise to the research.

slides.job: Deepen the distinction between contributing context and supplying a finished recommendation.
slides.text:
You don't need to arrive with a finished campaign idea.

Explaining what you hear is enough to start.
In this exchange, the client suggested something worth a look, and we agreed to investigate it.

slides.job: Close for both management and guided-launch readers without an explicit CTA.
slides.text:
Whether you want our team to manage your ads, or to launch your campaigns and guide you while you run them, what you know about your couples belongs in the partnership.

We want our expertise working with it.

caption.body:
When you already market your venue, you spend a lot of time with the couples considering it. You hear how they talk about the area, what they call it and how well they know it. And when you bring in advertising specialists, you want that experience to count for something.

A keyword discussion with a venue client gives a small example. We reviewed the terms already in place and our proposed additions, then invited her perspective. She raised the abbreviation people use for the region and described its familiarity among locals and some couples visiting from elsewhere.

We agreed to investigate and pass along any further terms we found. The client contributed the context, and our team committed to the research.

We believe the value of that conversation reaches past the suggestion itself. It shows how a prepared recommendation can become a useful discussion with someone who knows the market firsthand.

Owners who invest in specialist support should be able to bring that experience in while the strategy is being considered, with a clear role for the expertise on each side.
caption.hook: Being asked to approve a Google keyword list is different from being invited to add to it.
caption.ending: If you're investing in Google Ads, we think that's a fair thing to expect from the team you hire.

content.title: The shorthand a venue client raised in her keyword review
content.script:
A venue client gave our team another phrase to investigate for her Google Ads.

Here's what happened. Our team was reviewing the keywords she already had, along with some additional recommendations. And they asked whether she had any questions or concerns about the list.

She brought up the shorthand people use for her area. She explained that local people use it, and some couples from outside the area do, too. And if couples say it, some of them might be searching it, too. And that's exactly the kind of term that's easy to miss when the list is built from the outside.

Our team said they'd look into it and share any other terms they found.

What stands out to me is how she contributed. She brought something she knew about the way people talk about her market into the research conversation.

When you're speaking with couples, you're hearing language that can be useful to the people working on your ads. We bring our advertising expertise, and you bring that firsthand experience.

I think a good partnership should give both a place in the strategy, so your knowledge of couples can help shape what our team explores.

caption.body:
If you're paying for Google Ads, you want specialists who bring a considered recommendation to the table. You also have knowledge of your market that comes from speaking directly with the people choosing a wedding venue.

Those contributions can work together. During a keyword review, our team asked a venue client for questions about the existing terms and the additions being proposed. She suggested looking into a familiar abbreviation for her area, explaining that people used it locally and that it was familiar to some couples traveling in, too. If couples use a name like that in conversation, some may use it when they search.

Our team agreed to research the suggestion and share any further terms they found. Her contribution gave the team another question to pursue.

We believe that kind of exchange belongs in an advertising partnership. The research gives the conversation a starting point, while the client's experience can add something worth exploring. For an owner who already knows the market well, expert support should offer a useful place for that knowledge.
caption.hook: The person talking with your couples has something to add to your Google Ads.
caption.ending:
If you're already investing in Google Ads, the team supporting you should be asking what you hear from couples, and looking into what you tell them.

-Whitney

Close on a partnership that combines recommendations with the client's experience.
content.title: Your knowledge of couples belongs in the strategy
content.script:
I think the way your couples talk about your area should have a place in your Google Ads strategy.

If you're the one talking with couples, you hear the words they use for your area and for where they want to get married. That's useful to an advertising team, even after we've prepared our recommendations.

Here's a small example. In a keyword review, our team invited a venue client's questions about the list, and she suggested looking into the common shorthand for her region. She explained that locals use it, and so do some couples who aren't from there. Our team agreed to look into it and share anything else they found.

To me, that's what a useful advertising partnership should feel like.

You're hiring us for our expertise, and we take that seriously. You also know your couples in a way we can't from the outside, and both of those belong in the same conversation.

So we bring recommendations worth discussing, and we leave room for what you've heard to shape what we look into next.

caption.body:
You already talk with the couples considering your venue. You hear how they describe the location, the names they use for it, and how well they know the area. When you bring in Google Ads specialists, none of that stops being valuable.

We believe an advertising partnership should put those two kinds of knowledge together. Our recommendations give us something concrete to discuss, and your perspective can help inform the research.

In a keyword review with one of our venue clients, our team invited her questions about the list. She raised the everyday shorthand for the region and explained that locals use it and that it's familiar to some visiting couples. The team committed to looking into her suggestion and sending along any additional findings.

She did more than approve the proposed terms. She contributed knowledge of her market that gave our team something else to investigate.

For owners who already advertise, that's the collaboration we want to offer: specialist support that takes your experience seriously and gives it a practical place in the work.
caption.hook: You can trust Google Ads specialists and still have something to add.
caption.ending:
You should be able to trust the team running your ads and still know your read on couples is welcome in the conversation.

-Whitney

caption.body:
You talk with local couples and couples planning from out of town, and you hear how they refer to your area. That perspective is worth bringing to Google Ads research, right alongside a specialist's recommendations.

In one client conversation, our team presented existing keywords and possible additions, then asked for input. The client pointed out a shortened name people use for the area. She explained that it was common locally and also familiar to some couples coming from elsewhere.

The next commitment came from our team: investigate the suggestion and share any other terms the research uncovered.

The client supplied the local context, and our team took responsibility for looking into it.

For an owner already investing in advertising, expert support should put that knowledge to work. A prepared keyword list can open a discussion where the person closest to the couples has something meaningful to add.
